title: A Simple, Nearly-Optimal Algorithm for Differentially Private All-Pairs Shortest Distances

candidates.exact_quote: In particular, we note that we do not release any shortest path trees themselves, hence no shortest path information is revealed.
candidates.claim_content:
Setting (all from the paper's Section 2 and Section 3): A weighted undirected connected graph $G=(V,E,w)$ with $n=|V|$. Two graphs $G=(V,E,w)$ and $G'=(V,E,\tilde w)$ with IDENTICAL topology $(V,E)$ are *neighboring* iff $\|w-\tilde w\|_1 \le 1$ (Definition 2.1). A mechanism $M$ is $\varepsilon$-DP iff for all neighboring $X,X'$ and all $S$, $\mathbb{P}[M(X)\in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\,\mathbb{P}[M(X')\in S]$ (Definition 2.3 with $\delta=0$). Basic composition (Lemma 2.1): $k$ mechanisms each $(\varepsilon/k)$-DP compose to $\varepsilon$-DP. The available tree primitive (Lemma 3.2, from [Sea16]) is: *given a tree $T_z=(V,E,w)$ with root $z$*, there is an $\varepsilon$-DP algorithm releasing $d_{T_z}(z,u)$ for every $u\in V$ that is $O(\log^{1.5}(n)\log(n/\gamma)/\varepsilon)$-accurate with probability $1-\gamma$; its proof adds Laplace noise $\mathrm{Lap}(\log(n)/\varepsilon)$ to centroid-decomposition distances of that tree, and its sensitivity-1 argument is taken with respect to the tree's FIXED edge set.

The claim to check: the algorithm of Theorem 3.1 samples a uniformly random hitting set $S\subseteq V$ with $|S|=s$, and *for each $z\in S$ grows a shortest path tree $T_z$ of $G$ rooted at $z$*, then applies the $\varepsilon/(2s)$-DP algorithm of Lemma 3.2 to each $T_z$ to release $\tilde d(z,u)$ for all $u\in V$; it also runs an $\varepsilon/2$-DP input-perturbation mechanism. The paper concludes by basic composition that the whole algorithm is $\varepsilon$-DP, justifying this with the assertion that no shortest path tree is itself released, hence no shortest-path information leaks.

Is the composed mechanism $\varepsilon$-DP? Note that the tree $T_z$ is a *shortest path tree of $G$*, i.e. it is a function of the private weight vector $w$: two neighboring graphs $G, G'$ with $\|w-w'\|_1\le 1$ can have different shortest path trees rooted at the same $z$ (e.g. a 4-cycle $z-a-x-b-z$ where the two $z$-to-$x$ routes have lengths differing by less than 1, so an $\ell_1$ perturbation of mass 1 flips which route the tree contains). Lemma 3.2's guarantee is stated and proved for a tree given as input, with noise calibrated to sensitivity 1 over that tree's fixed edge set. Does the output distribution of 'build the shortest path tree from $w$, then run Lemma 3.2 on it' satisfy the $\varepsilon$-DP inequality of Definition 2.3 with respect to neighboring $w$?
candidates.suspected_defect: The privacy proof treats the shortest path trees $T_z$ as public/fixed input to Lemma 3.2, but each $T_z$ is computed from the private edge weights $w$. Lemma 3.2's noise is calibrated to sensitivity 1 over a FIXED tree; when the tree's topology is itself a function of $w$, the output distribution can change discontinuously between neighboring graphs and the $e^{\varepsilon}$ bound of Definition 2.3 need not hold. The paper's stated justification ('we do not release any shortest path trees themselves') does not address this: the released distances depend on the data-dependent tree structure, so the leak is through the distances, not through an explicit release of the tree. Definition 2.1 makes only the graph topology $(V,E)$ public, not the shortest-path-tree topology. If this is right, the $\varepsilon$-DP claim of Theorem 3.1 (and of Theorem 3.2, whose proof is stated to be identical) is unproved as written.

candidates.exact_quote: To achieve our upper bound for the accuracy, we note that each distance d̃_{G̃}^{(t)}(u, v) is the sum of a maximum of t edge weights, hence the total error in the estimate d̃^{(t)}(u, v) is the accumulation of at most t Laplace random variables.
candidates.claim_content:
Definitions (from the paper's Section 3): $G=(V,E,w)$ is a weighted undirected graph with $n=|V|$; $h(u,v)$ is the hop length (number of edges) of the shortest unweighted path; $d_G^{(t)}(u,v)$ is the minimum weight of a $u$-$v$ path using at most $t$ edges ($=\infty$ if $h(u,v)>t$). The algorithm forms $\tilde G=(V,E,\tilde w)$ with $\tilde w_e = w_e + Y_e$, $Y_e \sim \mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)$ independently for every edge $e\in E$, and outputs $\tilde d^{(t)}(u,v) := d_{\tilde G}^{(t)}(u,v)$, i.e. the minimum over all $u$-$v$ paths with at most $t$ edges of the NOISY path weight. Available concentration tool (Lemma 2.4, [CSS11]): if $X_1,\dots,X_t$ are independent $\mathrm{Lap}(b)$ and $X=\sum_i X_i$ then for all $\gamma\in(0,1)$, $\mathbb{P}[|X| \ge O(b\sqrt{t}\log(1/\gamma))] \le \gamma$ — a bound for a FIXED, pre-specified set of $t$ summands.

The claim to check (Lemma 3.1): for $t\in\mathbb{N}$, $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$, $\gamma\in(0,0.5]$, with probability $1-\gamma$,
$$\max_{u,v\in V} |\tilde d^{(t)}(u,v) - d_G^{(t)}(u,v)| \le O\!\left(\sqrt{t}\,\log(n/\gamma)/\varepsilon\right).$$
The proof argues only that a $t$-hop distance is a sum of at most $t$ edge weights, so its error is a sum of at most $t$ independent $\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)$ variables, and applies Lemma 2.4 with failure probability $\gamma/n^2$ followed by a union bound over the $n^2$ pairs.

The quantity to examine is the lower-deviation direction. Write $P^\star$ for a true optimal $\le t$-hop $u$-$v$ path and $\tilde P$ for the path attaining the minimum in $d_{\tilde G}^{(t)}(u,v)$. Then $\tilde d^{(t)}(u,v) - d_G^{(t)}(u,v) \le \sum_{e\in P^\star} Y_e$, whose $t$ summands are fixed in advance; but $d_G^{(t)}(u,v) - \tilde d^{(t)}(u,v) \le -\sum_{e\in \tilde P} Y_e$, where $\tilde P$ is selected AFTER the noise is drawn, as the minimiser over as many as $n^{t-1}$ candidate $\le t$-hop paths. Does the stated $O(\sqrt{t}\log(n/\gamma)/\varepsilon)$ bound follow, or does controlling $\min_P \sum_{e\in P} Y_e$ over all $\le t$-hop paths force a union bound over $n^{\Theta(t)}$ paths (hence $\log(1/\gamma')=\Theta(t\log n)$ in Lemma 2.4, giving $O(t^{1.5}\log(n)/\varepsilon)$) or an edge-wise bound (giving $O(t\log(n/\gamma)/\varepsilon)$)?
candidates.suspected_defect: Lemma 2.4 is a concentration bound for a FIXED set of $t$ independent Laplace variables, but the path realising $d_{\tilde G}^{(t)}(u,v)$ is chosen after the noise is seen, i.e. it is the minimiser over exponentially many $\le t$-hop paths. The proof's 'the error is the accumulation of at most $t$ Laplace random variables' therefore appears to apply concentration to a data-dependent selection. A correct union bound over the up to $n^{t-1}$ candidate paths would give $O(\sqrt{t}\cdot t\log n/\varepsilon)$, and the naive edge-wise bound gives $O(t\log(n/\gamma)/\varepsilon)$ — which is exactly the $\tilde O(t/\varepsilon)$ bound the paper says previous work obtained and that this lemma claims to improve to $\tilde O(\sqrt{t}/\varepsilon)$. The claimed $\sqrt{t}$ saving is the source of the headline $\tilde O(n^{1/3}/\varepsilon)$ and $\tilde O(n^{1/4}/\varepsilon)$ bounds (via $t=\lceil 10(n/s)\log n\rceil$), so if the $\sqrt{t}$ is not justified the main accuracy results degrade.

candidates.error_location: Proof of Theorem 4.3 (Section 4.2), the step 'By equivalent logic, v ∈ C^m(w)'
candidates.claim_content:
Definitions (Section 4.2 of the paper). $G=(V,E,w)$ connected, $n=|V|$, $d(\cdot,\cdot)=d_G(\cdot,\cdot)$, and for $S\subseteq V$, $d(v,S)=\min_{u\in S} d(v,u)$. Fix $2\le k\le \lfloor \log n/\log 2\rfloor$ and $t=\lceil 100 n^{1/k}\log n\rceil$. For each $r\in[t]$ nested sets $A^r_{k-1}\subseteq\dots\subseteq A^r_1$ are sampled with $|A^r_i| = n^{1-(i+1)/k}$, and $A_i=\bigcup_{r\in[t]} A^r_i$. For $w\in A^r_i$ the (modified) cluster is $C^r(w)=\{x\in V: d(w,x) < d(x, A^r_i\setminus\{w\})\}$. Pivots: $p_i(u)\in A_i$ with $d(u,p_i(u))=d(u,A_i)$ (and $p_i(u)\leftarrow p_{i+1}(u)$ if $d(u,A_i)=d(u,A_{i+1})$). Bunches: $w\in B(u)$ iff $d(w,u) < d(u,p_{i+1}(u))$ for the level $i$ with $w\in A_i$. Lemma 4.6: $p_i(u)\in B(u)$ for all $i,u$. Lemma 4.5: for all $i\in[k-2]$, $r\in[t]$, $x\in V$, IF $w\in A^r_i$ is the closest vertex of $A^r_i$ to $x$ in $G$, THEN $d(x,p_{i+1}(x)) \le d(x, A^r_i\setminus\{w\})$ (with probability $\ge 1-1/n^2$ jointly). The estimate for a pair $u,v$ is produced by the Thorup–Zwick swapping procedure: start with $w=u$, $i=0$; while $w\notin B(v)$ set $i\leftarrow i+1$, swap $u$ and $v$, and set $w\leftarrow p_i(u)$; on stopping, output $\tilde d(u,v)=\tilde d_{T}(w,u)+\tilde d_{T}(w,v)$ for a tree $T$ of the collection.

The claim to check: on termination, with $w\in A^m_l$ for some $m\in[t]$, $l\in[k-1]$, the proof of Theorem 4.3 deduces $u\in C^m(w)$ from $w\in B(u)$ (Lemma 4.6) plus Lemma 4.5, and then asserts that *the same reasoning gives* $v\in C^m(w)$ from the stopping condition $w\in B(v)$. Both memberships are needed, because they are what puts both $d(w,u)$ and $d(w,v)$ inside the single tree $T^m_l$ that spans $C^m(w)$.

Point to examine: on termination $w=p_l(u)$ is by construction the closest vertex of $A_l \supseteq A^m_l$ to $u$, so $w$ is the closest vertex of $A^m_l$ to $u$ and Lemma 4.5's hypothesis holds for $x=u$. Does Lemma 4.5's hypothesis hold for $x=v$? Is $w=p_l(u)$ necessarily the closest vertex of $A^m_l$ to $v$? If some $w'\in A^m_l\setminus\{w\}$ satisfies $d(v,w')\le d(v,w)$, then $d(v, A^m_l\setminus\{w\}) \le d(v,w)$, so the defining inequality $d(w,v) < d(v, A^m_l\setminus\{w\})$ of $v\in C^m(w)$ fails.
candidates.suspected_defect: Lemma 4.5 is conditional on '$w\in A^r_i$ is the closest to $u$ in $G$'. On termination of the swapping procedure $w=p_l(u)$ is the closest vertex of $A_l$ (hence of $A^m_l$) to $u$, so the hypothesis holds for $u$ — but there is nothing making $w$ the closest vertex of $A^m_l$ to $v$, and $v$ is the OTHER endpoint, reached only via the stopping condition $w\in B(v)$. If some $w'\in A^m_l\setminus\{w\}$ is at least as close to $v$ as $w$ is, then $d(v,A^m_l\setminus\{w\})\le d(v,w)$ and $v\notin C^m(w)$ by the definition of the modified cluster. So 'by equivalent logic' appears to invoke Lemma 4.5 outside the condition under which it was stated. This membership is load-bearing: without $v\in C^m(w)$ there is no single tree $T^\star\in\mathbf{T}$ containing both $d(w,u)$ and $d(w,v)$, and the identity $\tilde d(u,v)=d_{T^\star}(w,u)+d_{T^\star}(w,v)$ used to transfer the $(2k-1)$ stretch of Lemma 4.7 to the released estimates breaks.

candidates.exact_quote: max_{u,v∈V} |d_T(u, v) − 𝑑̃_T(u, v)| ≤ O(k · n^{1/k} · log^{1.5}(n) · log(n · t · k/γ)/ε)
candidates.claim_content:
Inputs (Section 4.2 of the paper). The collection of spanning trees is $\mathbf{T}=\{T^r_i\}$ with exactly one tree per set $A^r_i$, and the paper states $|\mathbf{T}| = t\cdot k$ where $t=\lceil 100\, n^{1/k}\log(n)\rceil$, i.e. $|\mathbf{T}| = \Theta(k\, n^{1/k}\log n)$. The per-tree primitive is Corollary 4.1: for a tree $T=(V,E,w)$, $\varepsilon'\in(0,1]$, $\gamma'\in(0,0.5]$, there is an $\varepsilon'$-DP algorithm releasing all-pairs distances in $T$ that is $O(\log^{1.5}(n)\log(n/\gamma')/\varepsilon')$-accurate with probability $1-\gamma'$. The proof of Theorem 4.3 runs, for every $T\in\mathbf{T}$, the $\varepsilon/(t\cdot k)$-DP algorithm of Corollary 4.1, and takes a union bound over all $t\cdot k$ trees, i.e. it uses $\varepsilon' = \varepsilon/(t k)$ and $\gamma' = \gamma/(t k)$. Proposition E.2 of the paper states (1) $\log(\alpha^{1+\lambda}/\gamma)=O(\log(\alpha/\gamma))$ and (2) $\log(\alpha/\gamma)=O(\log(\alpha)\log(1/\gamma))$ for $\alpha\ge2$, $\gamma\in(0,0.5]$, $\lambda>0$.

The claim to check is the first displayed line of (3):
$$\max_{u,v\in V}|d_T(u,v)-\tilde d_T(u,v)| \le O\!\left(k\cdot n^{1/k}\cdot \log^{1.5}(n)\cdot \log(n\,t\,k/\gamma)/\varepsilon\right)$$
and the conclusion of Theorem 4.3 that the algorithm is $(2k-1,\ O(k\, n^{1/k}\log^{2.5}(n)\log(k)\log(1/\gamma)/\varepsilon))$-accurate.

Substituting $\varepsilon'=\varepsilon/(tk)$ into Corollary 4.1 gives accuracy $O(t\,k\,\log^{1.5}(n)\log(n t k/\gamma)/\varepsilon)$, and $t k = \Theta(k\, n^{1/k}\log n)$. Does the displayed prefactor $k\,n^{1/k}\log^{1.5}(n)$ equal $t\,k\,\log^{1.5}(n)$, or is it smaller by a factor $\Theta(\log n)$? For comparison, the analogous step in the proof of Theorem 4.1 uses $|\mathbf{T}|=k n^{1/k}$ (no $\log n$ factor, from Lemma 4.1) and there the prefactor $k n^{1/k}\log^{1.5}(n)$ is exactly $|\mathbf{T}|\log^{1.5}(n)$.
candidates.suspected_defect: The per-tree privacy budget is $\varepsilon/(t\cdot k)$ with $t\cdot k = \Theta(k\,n^{1/k}\log n)$, so Corollary 4.1 yields $O(t k \log^{1.5}(n)\log(ntk/\gamma)/\varepsilon) = O(k\,n^{1/k}\,\log^{2.5}(n)\,\log(n t k/\gamma)/\varepsilon)$ — but the displayed line writes the prefactor as $k\,n^{1/k}\,\log^{1.5}(n)$, apparently substituting $|\mathbf{T}| = k n^{1/k}$ (the Construction-1 count of Theorem 4.1) instead of $t\cdot k = 100 k n^{1/k}\log n$. The $\log n$ hidden in $t$ seems to be dropped, so the stated additive error of Theorem 4.3 (and of the abstract's $\tilde O(k\cdot n^{1/k}/\varepsilon)$ for Construction 2) looks short by one factor of $\log n$: $\log^{3.5}(n)$ rather than $\log^{2.5}(n)\log(k)$. The polynomial-in-$n$ factor $k n^{1/k}$ is unaffected, so the headline comparison with [CGK+23] survives.

candidates.error_location: Section 4.2 / proof of Theorem 4.3, privacy argument for the trees T_i^r
candidates.exact_quote: For each T ∈ T and u, v ∈ V, we run the ε/(t·k)-DP algorithm given by Corollary 4.1 to release the private distance estimates 𝑑̃_T(u, v) and let 𝑑̃(u, v) ← min_{T∈T} 𝑑̃_T(u, v).
candidates.claim_content:
Setting. Neighboring graphs share the topology $(V,E)$ and satisfy $\|w-\tilde w\|_1\le 1$ (Definition 2.1); $\varepsilon$-DP is Definition 2.3 with $\delta=0$; basic composition is Lemma 2.1. Corollary 4.1 states: *given a tree $T=(V,E,w)$*, there is an $\varepsilon'$-DP algorithm releasing all-pairs distances in $T$ with additive error $O(\log^{1.5}(n)\log(n/\gamma)/\varepsilon')$ w.p. $1-\gamma$; its proof roots $T$ at an arbitrary $z$, invokes Lemma 3.2 (Laplace noise on a centroid decomposition of the FIXED tree $T$), and computes $d_T(x,y)=\tilde d(z,x)+\tilde d(z,y)-2\tilde d(z,v_{x,y})$ using the lowest common ancestor $v_{x,y}$ of $x,y$ in $T$.

How $\mathbf{T}$ is built in Section 4.2: for each $r\in[t]$ and level $i$, $T^r_i$ starts as $(V,\emptyset)$; for every centre $w\in A^r_i$ the edges of the *shortest path tree of $G$ centred at $w$ and spanning the cluster* $C^r(w)=\{x: d_G(w,x)<d_G(x,A^r_i\setminus\{w\})\}$ are added; the resulting forest is completed to a spanning tree of $G$ by a Kruskal-style pass that repeatedly adds the smallest-weight remaining edge of $E(G)\setminus E(T^r_i)$ that creates no cycle.

The claim to check: that running, for each $T\in\mathbf{T}$, the $\varepsilon/(t k)$-DP algorithm of Corollary 4.1 and outputting $\tilde d(u,v)=\min_{T\in\mathbf{T}}\tilde d_T(u,v)$ is $\varepsilon$-DP by basic composition. Note that both the cluster memberships $C^r(w)$ (defined by comparisons of $G$-distances, i.e. of the private weights $w$) and the Kruskal completion (which picks the smallest-weight edges) make the vertex partition and the edge set of each $T^r_i$ a function of the private weight vector; Corollary 4.1's noise is calibrated to a tree supplied as fixed input. Does the $e^{\varepsilon}$ inequality of Definition 2.3 hold for the composed mechanism when the trees themselves depend on $w$?
candidates.suspected_defect: Corollary 4.1 (via Lemma 3.2) is an $\varepsilon'$-DP mechanism for a tree given as public input; its sensitivity-1 argument is taken over that tree's fixed edge set and its post-processing uses the tree's fixed LCA structure. But every $T^r_i$ in Section 4.2 is derived from the private weights: the clusters $C^r(w)$ are defined by inequalities between $G$-distances, the within-cluster trees are shortest path trees of $G$, and the Kruskal completion selects minimum-weight edges. Neighboring weight vectors can therefore yield different trees, and the privacy accounting of basic composition over $t\cdot k$ calls does not cover that data dependence. Same structural concern as the Theorem 3.1 privacy step, at a different location and for a different tree family; if it is real, the $\varepsilon$-DP claims of Theorems 4.3 and 4.4 are unproved as written. (Theorem 4.1's Construction 1 inherits the same concern through the weight-dependent tree-padding spanner of Lemma 4.1.)

candidates.exact_quote: Furthermore, we define the bunches as B(u) = {w ∈ V | d(w, u) < d(u, p_{i+1}(u))}.
candidates.claim_content:
Context (Section 4.2). $V=A_0\supseteq A_1\supseteq\dots\supseteq A_{k-1}$ with $A_k=\emptyset$; for each $i\in[k-1]$ the pivot $p_i(u)\in A_i$ satisfies $d_G(u,p_i(u))=d_G(u,A_i)$, with $p_i(u)\leftarrow p_{i+1}(u)$ when $d(u,A_i)=d(u,A_{i+1})$; $d(v,S)=\min_{x\in S}d(v,x)$ and $d(u,A_k)=\infty$.

The definition to check, exactly as the paper writes it: $B(u) = \{w\in V \mid d(w,u) < d(u, p_{i+1}(u))\}$. The index $i$ is not quantified or bound anywhere in this definition — it appears free on the right-hand side while the left-hand side depends only on $u$. In the construction this definition is used by: Lemma 4.6 ('for all $i\in[k-1]$ and $u\in V$, $p_i(u)\in B(u)$', whose proof splits on $d(u,A_i)=d(u,A_{i+1})$ versus $d(u,A_i)<d(u,A_{i+1})$); the stopping test $w\in B(v)$ of the swapping procedure; the claim $A_{k-1}\subseteq B(v)$ for every $v$; and the step of Lemma 4.7 that reads '$w_{i-1}\notin B(v_{i-1})$, so $d(w_{i-1},v_{i-1})\ge d(A_i,v_{i-1}) = d(p_i(v_{i-1}),v_{i-1})$'. The corresponding definition in Thorup–Zwick [TZ05], which this construction says it follows, is level-indexed: $B(u) = \bigcup_{i=0}^{k-1}\{w\in A_i\setminus A_{i+1} : d(w,u) < d(u, A_{i+1})\}$. Is the paper's definition well-formed as stated, and is it the one its own uses require?
candidates.suspected_defect: The definition of $B(u)$ contains a free index $i$ that is neither quantified nor tied to $w$, so as written the set is not well-defined — it would read differently for each choice of $i$. Every use of it in the construction implicitly reads $i$ as 'the level of $w$', i.e. $w\in A_i\setminus A_{i+1}$, which is the Thorup–Zwick definition $d(w,u)<d(u,A_{i+1})$. Under a single global $i$ the downstream claims break (e.g. $A_{k-1}\subseteq B(v)$, which needs $i=k-1$ and $d(v,A_k)=\infty$, and Lemma 4.7's step, which needs $i$ to be the current iteration index). This is a definitional defect rather than a false numeric claim, but the definition is falsifiable and load-bearing for Lemmas 4.6, 4.7 and Theorem 4.3.

candidates.error_location: Proof of Lemma 4.4 (Section 4.2), the step E[X_i] > (t/2)|A^r_i|
candidates.exact_quote: where the first inequality follows from Bernoulli's inequality, and the last inequality follows from |A^r_i| · t ≤ n.
candidates.claim_content:
Setting (Section 4.2). $n=|V|$, integer $k$ with $2\le k\le\lfloor\log(n)/\log 2\rfloor$ (so $n^{1/k}\ge2$), and $t=\lceil 100\,n^{1/k}\log(n)\rceil$. For $i\in[k-1]$ and $r\in[t]$, $|A^r_i| = n^{1-(i+1)/k}$ and $A_i=\bigcup_{r\in[t]}A^r_i$. Each vertex independently-across-$r$ has $\mathbb{P}[u\in A^r_i]=|A^r_i|/n$ (Lemma 4.3), so $p_i = 1-(1-|A^r_i|/n)^t$ and $X_i\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p_i)$ counts $|A_i|$.

The chain to check is
$$\mathbb{E}[X_i] = n\left(1-(1-|A^r_i|/n)^t\right) \ \ge\ n\left(1-\frac{1}{1+|A^r_i|t/n}\right) \ =\ \frac{t}{1+|A^r_i|t/n}\cdot|A^r_i| \ >\ (t/2)\cdot|A^r_i| = (t/2)\,n^{1-(i+1)/k},$$
where the paper justifies the first inequality by Bernoulli's inequality and the last one by the assertion $|A^r_i|\cdot t \le n$.

The side condition to examine is exactly that assertion. Substituting the paper's own values, $|A^r_i|\cdot t = n^{1-(i+1)/k}\cdot\lceil 100\,n^{1/k}\log n\rceil \ge 100\,n^{1-i/k}\log(n)$, which for $i=1$ is $100\,n^{1-1/k}\log(n)$. So $|A^r_i| t \le n$ requires $100\log(n)\le n^{1/k}$. Does that hold for every $k$ in the admitted range $2\le k\le\lfloor\log(n)/\log 2\rfloor$ — in particular at the upper end, where $n^{1/k}\to 2$?
candidates.suspected_defect: The step $\mathbb{E}[X_i] > (t/2)|A^r_i|$ needs $1+|A^r_i|t/n \le 2$, i.e. $|A^r_i|\cdot t\le n$, which the proof asserts without derivation. With the paper's $t=\lceil 100 n^{1/k}\log n\rceil$ and $|A^r_1|=n^{1-2/k}$, the product at level $i=1$ is $\Theta(n^{1-1/k}\log n)$, so the condition amounts to $100\log(n)\lesssim n^{1/k}$. That fails throughout the upper part of the paper's own admitted range $k\le\lfloor\log(n)/\log(2)\rfloor$, where $n^{1/k}$ is as small as $2$ while $100\log n$ grows without bound; e.g. $n=2^{20}$, $k=20$ gives $n^{1/k}=2$ and $|A^r_1|t \approx 100\cdot 2\cdot 2^{19}\log(n) \gg n$. If the condition fails, the constant-factor loss in $\mathbb{E}[X_i]$ is larger than $2$ and the conclusion $|A_i|\ge(t/4)n^{1-(i+1)/k}$ of Lemma 4.4 — which feeds the exponent in the Lemma 4.5 failure-probability bound — does not follow as stated for those $k$.

candidates.error_location: Proof of Lemma 4.5 (Section 4.2), the product-form probability bounds
candidates.exact_quote: the probability that all the vertices in A^r_i - {w} come after v, or O_u(y) > O_u(v) for all y ∈ A^r_i - {w}, is (1 - j/n)^{|A^r_i|-1}
candidates.suspected_defect: Two product-form steps substitute independence for dependence. (i) $(1-j/n)^{|A^r_i|-1}$ treats the $|A^r_i|-1$ members of $A^r_i\setminus\{w\}$ as i.i.d. uniform vertices, but they are drawn without replacement and the draw is conditioned on $A^r_{i+1}\subseteq A^r_i$ and on $v$'s own position. (ii) $(1-1/(2|A^r_i|))^{|A_{i+1}|}$ treats the $|A_{i+1}|$ events '$v$ precedes all of $A^r_i\setminus\{w\}$' as independent across $v\in A_{i+1}$, but they all concern the same random set $A^r_i$, and $A_{i+1}$ and $A^r_i$ are not independent since $A^r_{i+1}\subseteq A^r_i\cap A_{i+1}$. Neither step is accompanied by a negative-association or conditioning argument. The exponentiated bound is what produces the $1-n^{-7}$ failure probability and hence the $1-1/n^2$ guarantee of Lemma 4.5, which Theorem 4.3 relies on for the cluster memberships.

candidates.exact_quote: The proof is the same as Theorem 4.3, except we run the $\varepsilon/(2\sqrt{2}(t\cdot k) \cdot \log(2/\delta))$-DP algorithm given by Corollary 4.1 to release private APSD $\tilde{d}_{\mathcal{T}}(u, v)$ for each $\mathcal{T} \in \mathbb{T}$.
candidates.claim_content:
Inputs. $|\mathbf{T}| = t\cdot k$ with $t=\lceil 100\,n^{1/k}\log n\rceil$, so $|\mathbf{T}|=\Theta(k\,n^{1/k}\log n)$. Advanced composition (Lemma 2.2 of the paper): running $K$ mechanisms each $\big(\varepsilon/(2\sqrt{2K\log(2/\delta)}),\ \delta/(2K)\big)$-DP is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP. Corollary 4.1: for a tree $T$, an $\varepsilon'$-DP algorithm releases all-pairs distances in $T$ with error $O(\log^{1.5}(n)\log(n/\gamma')/\varepsilon')$ w.p. $1-\gamma'$. Proposition E.2: $\log(\alpha^{1+\lambda}/\gamma)=O(\log(\alpha/\gamma))$ and $\log(\alpha/\gamma)=O(\log\alpha\cdot\log(1/\gamma))$.

The claim to check (Theorem 4.4): for $\gamma\in(0,0.5]$, $\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1]$ and $k\in\{2,\dots,\lfloor\log(n)/\log 2\rfloor\}$ there is an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP algorithm for APSD that is
$$\Big(2k-1,\ O\big(\sqrt{k}\cdot n^{1/(2k)}\cdot\log^{2.5}(n)\cdot\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}\cdot\log(k)\cdot\log(1/\gamma)/\varepsilon\big)\Big)\text{-accurate}$$
with probability $1-\gamma-1/n^2$.

Computation to reproduce: with $K=t k$, advanced composition sets $1/\varepsilon' = \Theta\big(\sqrt{K\log(2/\delta)}/\varepsilon\big) = \Theta\big(\sqrt{k\,n^{1/k}\log(n)\log(2/\delta)}/\varepsilon\big) = \Theta\big(\sqrt{k}\,n^{1/(2k)}\sqrt{\log n}\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}/\varepsilon\big)$. Multiplying by Corollary 4.1's $\log^{1.5}(n)\log(n/\gamma')$ and simplifying by Proposition E.2, is the resulting exponent of $\log(n)$ equal to the claimed $2.5$, or is it $3$?
candidates.suspected_defect: The per-tree budget is obtained by advanced composition over $|\mathbf{T}|=t\cdot k = \Theta(k\,n^{1/k}\log n)$ trees, so $1/\varepsilon'$ carries a factor $\sqrt{\log n}$ from $t$ in addition to $\sqrt{k}\,n^{1/(2k)}$. Multiplying by Corollary 4.1's $\log^{1.5}(n)$ and the simplified $\log(n t k/\gamma)=O(\log(n)\log(k)\log(1/\gamma))$ gives $\log^{3}(n)$, not the claimed $\log^{2.5}(n)$. This is the $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ counterpart of the same apparently dropped $t$-factor as in inequality (3) of Theorem 4.3; the polynomial factor $\sqrt{k}\,n^{1/(2k)}$ is unaffected, so only a polylogarithmic factor is at stake.

candidates.error_location: Section 1.3 (Algorithms with Additive and Multiplicative Approximations) vs Theorems 4.2 and 4.4
candidates.exact_quote: reducing the additive error to $O(\sqrt{k n^{1/(2k)}}/\varepsilon)$
candidates.claim_content:
The paper states the additive error of its Construction 1 in the $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP setting in three places. (i) The abstract: '$\tilde O(\sqrt{k}\cdot n^{1/(2k)}/\varepsilon)$ in the $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP case'. (ii) Section 1.3: 'we use advanced composition to release the distance estimates computed within each tree, exactly as in the previous section, reducing the additive error to $O(\sqrt{k n^{1/(2k)}}/\varepsilon)$', and for Construction 2 in the same section: 'our total algorithm is $(2k-1,\tilde O(kn^{1/k}))$-accurate in the $\varepsilon$-DP case and $(2k-1, O(\sqrt{kn^{1/(2k)}}))$-accurate in the $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP case'. (iii) Theorem 4.2: additive error $O(\sqrt{k}\cdot n^{1/(2k)}\cdot\log^{2.5}(n)\cdot\log(k)\cdot\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}\cdot\log(1/\gamma)/\varepsilon)$; and Theorem 4.4: additive error $O(\sqrt{k}\cdot n^{1/(2k)}\cdot\log^{2.5}(n)\cdot\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}\cdot\log(k)\cdot\log(1/\gamma)/\varepsilon)$.

The question is whether $\sqrt{k\,n^{1/(2k)}}$ and $\sqrt{k}\cdot n^{1/(2k)}$ denote the same quantity, and if not which is implied by the mechanism. The mechanism applies advanced composition (Lemma 2.2: $K$ mechanisms each $\varepsilon/(2\sqrt{2K\log(2/\delta)})$-DP compose to $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP) across $K=k\,n^{1/k}$ trees (Lemma 4.1), so the additive error scales as $1/\varepsilon' = \Theta(\sqrt{K\log(2/\delta)}/\varepsilon) = \Theta(\sqrt{k\,n^{1/k}\log(2/\delta)}/\varepsilon)$. Simplify $\sqrt{k\,n^{1/k}}$ and compare with each of the two written forms.
candidates.suspected_defect: $\sqrt{k\,n^{1/(2k)}} = \sqrt{k}\cdot n^{1/(4k)}$, which is NOT the same as $\sqrt{k}\cdot n^{1/(2k)}$. Deriving the bound from advanced composition over $K=k\,n^{1/k}$ trees gives $\sqrt{K} = \sqrt{k}\,n^{1/(2k)}$, matching the abstract and Theorems 4.2/4.4; the Section 1.3 forms $O(\sqrt{k n^{1/(2k)}}/\varepsilon)$ and $(2k-1, O(\sqrt{kn^{1/(2k)}}))$ therefore state a strictly smaller additive error than the theorems they summarise. Internal inconsistency between the overview and the formal statements; it reads like a misplaced radical, but as written Section 1.3 claims an $n^{1/(4k)}$ dependence that no theorem in the paper proves.

candidates.claim_content:

The sets built are $A^r_i$ for $r\in[t]$ and $i\in[k-1]$ (the paper writes 'Lastly, we let $A_i = \cup_r A^r_i$ for each $i \in [k-1]$', and the nested family is $V=A_0\supseteq A_1\supseteq\dots\supseteq A_{k-1}$, with $A_k=\emptyset$). (b) since $t=\lceil 100 n^{1/k}\log n\rceil$ is a ceiling, is $t\cdot k$ exactly equal to $100\,k\,n^{1/k}\log(n)$, or only at least that? candidates.error_location: Proof of Lemma 3.1 (Section 3), the displayed error inequality
candidates.claim_content:
Notation (Section 3 of the paper). $G=(V,E,w)$ is the true graph and $\tilde G=(V,E,\tilde w)$ the noisy graph with $\tilde w = w + (Y_e)_{e\in E}$, $Y_e\sim\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)$ i.i.d. $d_G^{(t)}(u,v)$ denotes the minimum weight of a $u$-$v$ path with at most $t$ edges in $G$. The algorithm of Lemma 3.1 'returns $\tilde d^{(t)}(u,v) \leftarrow \tilde d_{\tilde G}^{(t)}(u,v)$ for each $u,v\in V$', i.e. the output $\tilde d^{(t)}$ is BY DEFINITION the $t$-hop distance computed in $\tilde G$. The statement of Lemma 3.1 bounds $\max_{u,v\in V}|\tilde d^{(t)}(u,v) - d_G^{(t)}(u,v)|$, i.e. the deviation of the output from the TRUE $t$-hop distance.

The displayed line to check, inside the proof: 'By Lemma 2.4, with probability at least $1-\gamma/n^2$ we have, $|\tilde d^{(t)}(u,v) - d_{\tilde G}^{(t)}(u,v)| \le O(\sqrt{t}\log(n^2/\gamma)/\varepsilon) = O(\sqrt{t}\log(n/\gamma)/\varepsilon)$'. Evaluate the left-hand side given that $\tilde d^{(t)}(u,v)$ was defined as $d_{\tilde G}^{(t)}(u,v)$, and compare it with the quantity the lemma statement requires to be bounded.
candidates.suspected_defect: The displayed inequality bounds $|\tilde d^{(t)}(u,v) - d_{\tilde G}^{(t)}(u,v)|$, but $\tilde d^{(t)}(u,v)$ is defined two paragraphs earlier as exactly $d_{\tilde G}^{(t)}(u,v)$, so the left-hand side is identically $0$ and the inequality is vacuous. The quantity the proof needs — and that Lemma 3.1 states — is $|\tilde d^{(t)}(u,v) - d_G^{(t)}(u,v)|$, with the TRUE graph $G$ in the second term. A subscript slip rather than a false claim, but it means the proof's only displayed bound does not formally establish the lemma, and the same $G$ versus $\tilde G$ confusion recurs in Theorem 3.1, where the private estimate returned by Lemma 3.1 is also written $d_G^{(t)}(u,v)$.

candidates.error_location: Lemma 3.1 statement (Section 3), the maximum over all vertex pairs
candidates.claim_content:
Definitions (Section 3 of the paper, verbatim in content): $h(u,v)$ is the hop length between $u$ and $v$, i.e. $h(u,v)=d_{G'}(u,v)$ where $G'=(V,E,\{1\}^{|E|})$; and '$d_G^{(t)}(u,v)$ [is] the shortest $t$-hop path between $u$ and $v$ in the graph $G$, or the shortest path between $u$ and $v$ under the constraint of traversing at most $t$ edges. In particular, if $h(u,v) > t$, then $d_G^{(t)}(u,v) = \infty$.' The algorithm perturbs weights only, keeping the topology $(V,E)$ fixed, and outputs $\tilde d^{(t)}(u,v) = d_{\tilde G}^{(t)}(u,v)$, so $\tilde d^{(t)}(u,v)=\infty$ exactly when $d_G^{(t)}(u,v)=\infty$.

The claim to check (Lemma 3.1): for $t\in\mathbb{N}$, $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$, $\gamma\in(0,0.5]$, with probability $1-\gamma$,
$$\max_{u,v\in V} \big|\tilde d^{(t)}(u,v) - d_G^{(t)}(u,v)\big| \le O\!\left(\sqrt{t}\,\log(n/\gamma)/\varepsilon\right).$$
The maximum is taken over ALL pairs $u,v\in V$, with no restriction to pairs satisfying $h(u,v)\le t$. Evaluate the summand for a pair with $h(u,v)>t$ and decide whether the stated maximum is well-defined and whether the inequality can hold.
candidates.suspected_defect: The maximum ranges over all $u,v\in V$, but by the paper's own definition $d_G^{(t)}(u,v)=\infty$ whenever $h(u,v)>t$, and $\tilde d^{(t)}(u,v)=\infty$ for the same pairs (the topology is unperturbed). The summand is then $|\infty-\infty|$, which is undefined, so the stated maximum is ill-defined and the inequality cannot be read literally for a graph containing any pair at hop distance more than $t$. The statement needs to be restricted to pairs with $h(u,v)\le t$ (which is how Theorem 3.1 actually uses it, in Case B). A well-formedness defect in the lemma statement, not a false quantitative bound.

candidates.error_location: Proof of Lemma 3.2 (Appendix A), induction on the number of released distances
candidates.exact_quote: Hence, u ∈ Vᵢ for some i ∈ [t].
candidates.claim_content:
Setting (Appendix A of the paper). $T_z=(V,E,w)$ is a tree rooted at $z$ with $|V|=n$. The algorithm picks the centroid $z^\ast$ (the one closer to $z$ if there are two), lets $z_1,\dots,z_t$ be the children of $z^\ast$ with corresponding subtrees $T_i=(V_i,E_i)$ for $i\in\{1,\dots,t\}$, and additionally defines '$T_0$ to be the subtree rooted at $z$ with vertex set $V_0 = V - \{V_1,\dots,V_t\}$'. It releases $d(z,z^\ast)$ and $d(z^\ast,z_i)$ for each child with $\mathrm{Lap}(\log(n)/\varepsilon)$ noise, then recurses on each subtree. Here $[i]$ denotes $\{1,2,\dots,i\}$ (Section 4.2 of the paper), so $[t]=\{1,\dots,t\}$ excludes $0$.

The claim to check is the induction establishing that the number of released noisy distances composing $d(z,u)$ is at most $2\log(n)$: 'Suppose $n>1$. In the first iteration of the algorithm, the vertex sets $V_0, V_1, \dots, V_t$ are a partition of $V$. Hence, $u\in V_i$ for some $i\in[t]$. By the induction hypothesis, we can release the distance from $z_i$ to $u$ by the composition of at most $2\log(n/2) = 2\log(n)-2$ noisy distances. Then, we have that $d(z,z_i) = d(z,z^\ast)+d(z^\ast,z_i)$, giving a total of $2\log(n)$ noisy distances.'

Check whether the case distinction is exhaustive over the stated partition $V_0,V_1,\dots,V_t$, and whether the vertices of $V_0$ are covered by the displayed argument (which routes $u$ through $z^\ast$ and a child $z_i$).
candidates.suspected_defect: The partition is $V_0,V_1,\dots,V_t$ but the induction only considers $u\in V_i$ for $i\in[t]=\{1,\dots,t\}$, omitting the case $u\in V_0$ — the subtree containing the original root $z$. For $u\in V_0$ the displayed accounting ($d(z,z_i)=d(z,z^\ast)+d(z^\ast,z_i)$ plus the recursive distance from $z_i$) does not apply, since $u$ is not reached through $z^\ast$ and a child $z_i$ at all. The gap looks repairable (the recursive call on $T_0$ is rooted at $z$ and uses $2\log(n/2)$ distances, which is fewer than $2\log n$), so the $O(\log^{1.5}(n)\log(n/\gamma)/\varepsilon)$ conclusion of Lemma 3.2 should survive, but the induction as written does not cover the whole partition.

candidates.error_location: Proof of Lemma 4.4 (Section 4.2), the binomial model for |A_i|
candidates.exact_quote: Let $X_{i} \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p_{i})$ be the number of vertices in $A_{i}$.
candidates.claim_content:
Setting (Section 4.2). For each iteration $r\in[t]$ the set $A^r_i$ is built by sampling WITHOUT replacement: $A^r_{k-1}$ is a single uniformly random vertex, and for each level $A^r_i = A^r_{i+1} \cup (\text{$n^{1-(i+1)/k}-n^{1-(i+2)/k}$ vertices sampled uniformly from $V\setminus A^r_{i+1}$})$. The paper notes explicitly: 'In our sampling procedure, the sets $A^r_i$ are sampled without replacement, however, a single vertex can be sampled at the $i$th level in more than one iteration $r\in[t]$.' The iterations $r$ are mutually independent (Lemma 4.3). Then $A_i=\bigcup_{r\in[t]}A^r_i$, and for a fixed vertex $u$, $\mathbb{P}[u\in A_i] = 1-(1-|A^r_i|/n)^t =: p_i$.

The claim to check: '$X_i\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p_i)$ [is] the number of vertices in $A_i$', which the proof then feeds into the Chernoff bound of Lemma 2.5 ($\mathbb{P}[X\le\mathbb{E}[X]-\lambda]\le e^{-\lambda^2/(2\mathbb{E}[X])}$ for $X\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p)$) with $\lambda=\mathbb{E}[X_i]/2$, to conclude $\mathbb{P}[X_i\le\mathbb{E}[X_i]/2]\le e^{-\mathbb{E}[X_i]/8}$ and hence $|A_i|\ge(t/4)n^{1-(i+1)/k}$ with probability $\ge 1-1/(2n^3)$ per level. Is $|A_i|$ exactly Binomial$(n,p_i)$, i.e. are the $n$ indicator variables $\mathbf{1}[u\in A_i]$, $u\in V$, mutually independent?
candidates.suspected_defect: $|A_i|$ is a sum of $n$ indicators $\mathbf{1}[u\in A_i]$ that each have mean $p_i$ but are not independent: within a single iteration $r$ the set $A^r_i$ has a FIXED size $n^{1-(i+1)/k}$ and is sampled without replacement, so the indicators are negatively correlated, and the union over $r$ inherits that dependence. Calling $|A_i|$ a Binomial$(n,p_i)$ variable and applying the binomial Chernoff bound of Lemma 2.5 is therefore an unjustified distributional substitution. The direction is plausibly favourable — negatively associated indicators satisfy the same lower-tail Chernoff bound — but the proof gives no such argument, and the conclusion $|A_i|\ge(t/4)n^{1-(i+1)/k}$ is used as an exponent in Lemma 4.5.

candidates.error_location: Theorem 3.2 and its proof (Appendix B), dependence on log(2/delta)
candidates.claim_content:
Setting (Appendix B of the paper). The algorithm is Algorithm 1 with the tree releases done under advanced composition: $s=|S|$ shortest path trees, each handled by the $\varepsilon/(4\sqrt{2s\log(2/\delta)})$-DP algorithm of Lemma 3.2, giving $(\varepsilon/2,\delta)$-DP, composed with the $\varepsilon/2$-DP input perturbation algorithm. The two accuracy bounds are
$$(5)\quad \max_{z\in S,u\in V}|d_G(z,u)-\tilde d(z,u)| \le O\big(\sqrt{s}\,\log^{1.5}(n)\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}\,\log(2sn/\gamma)/\varepsilon\big),$$
$$(2)\quad |d(u,v)-d_G^{(t)}(u,v)| \le O\big(\sqrt{n/s}\,\log^{1.5}(n)\log(1/\gamma)/\varepsilon\big),$$
and the proof chooses $s=\sqrt{n}/(\log(n)\cdot\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)})$. Proposition E.2 gives $\log(\alpha^{1+\lambda}/\gamma)=O(\log(\alpha/\gamma))$ and $\log(\alpha/\gamma)=O(\log(\alpha)\log(1/\gamma))$.

The claim to check is the resulting bound $O(n^{1/4}\log^2(n)\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}\log(1/\gamma)/\varepsilon)$. Substitute the chosen $s$ into (5) and into (2) and simplify, tracking the exponent of $\log(2/\delta)$ in each: e.g. $\sqrt{s}\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)} = n^{1/4}\log^{-1/2}(n)\log^{-1/4}(2/\delta)\cdot\log^{1/2}(2/\delta) = n^{1/4}\log^{-1/2}(n)\log^{1/4}(2/\delta)$, and $\sqrt{n/s} = n^{1/4}\log^{1/2}(n)\log^{1/4}(2/\delta)$.
candidates.suspected_defect: Substituting $s=\sqrt{n}/(\log(n)\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)})$ into both (5) and (2) yields a $\log^{1/4}(2/\delta)$ dependence in each branch, whereas the displayed conclusion carries $\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)} = \log^{1/2}(2/\delta)$. The exponent of $\log(2/\delta)$ in the final bound does not appear to be the one the two balanced branches produce. As a big-$O$ upper bound the stated form is weaker, so the theorem as stated may still be true, but the $\delta$-dependence does not match the derivation and the optimal choice of $s$ would differ if the exponent is tracked correctly.

candidates.error_location: Section 3, sensitivity justification preceding the proof of Lemma 3.1
candidates.exact_quote: Since a shortest path cannot traverse any single edge more than once, the ℓ₁ sensitivity of a function that takes as input w and returns the shortest path distance between a pair of vertices is 1.
candidates.claim_content:
Definitions (Section 2 of the paper). Neighboring graphs: $G=(V,E,w)$ and $G'=(V,E,\tilde w)$ with equivalent topology are neighboring iff $\|w-\tilde w\|_1\le 1$ (Definition 2.1). $\ell_1$ sensitivity: $\Delta_1(f) := \max_{X,X'}\|f(X)-f(X')\|_1$ over neighboring $X,X'$, for $f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^D$ (Definition 2.2). Laplace mechanism (Lemma 2.3): for $f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^k$, sampling $Y_1,\dots,Y_k \sim \mathrm{Lap}(\Delta_1(f)/\varepsilon)$ independently and outputting $f(X)+(Y_1,\dots,Y_k)$ is $\varepsilon$-DP.

The argument to check, as the paper gives it: 'It is a simple application of the Laplace mechanism (Lemma 2.3) to the function $f: w\to\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ which takes as input the edge weights of a graph and outputs all-pairs shortest distances. [...] Since a shortest path cannot traverse any single edge more than once, the $\ell_1$ sensitivity of a function that takes as input $w$ and returns the shortest path distance between a pair of vertices is 1. Consequently, by Lemma 2.3, releasing the graph $\tilde G$ is $\varepsilon$-differentially private.' The algorithm itself adds $\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)$ to EVERY edge weight and releases the perturbed weight vector $\tilde w$, from which distances are post-processed.

Questions: (a) what is $\Delta_1$ of the map $f:w\mapsto(\text{all } n^2 \text{ shortest distances})$ under Definition 2.2 — is it $1$, or can it be as large as $\Theta(n^2)$? (b) does the per-pair sensitivity bound of $1$ justify the conclusion that releasing $\tilde G$ (i.e. applying the Laplace mechanism to the identity map on $w$, whose $\Delta_1$ is $1$ by Definition 2.1) is $\varepsilon$-DP?
candidates.suspected_defect: The sensitivity argument is a non sequitur for the mechanism actually used. The paper first names $f:w\to\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ returning all $n^2$ shortest distances, whose $\ell_1$ sensitivity under Definition 2.2 is the $\ell_1$ norm over all $n^2$ outputs and can be $\Theta(n^2)$, not $1$; it then bounds the sensitivity of the single-pair distance function (correctly $1$) and from that concludes that releasing the whole noisy graph $\tilde G$ is $\varepsilon$-DP. The conclusion is reachable — apply Lemma 2.3 to the identity map on $w$, which has $\Delta_1 = 1$ by Definition 2.1, so $\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)$ per edge suffices and the distances follow by post-processing — but that is not the argument given, and the per-pair sensitivity claim is not what licenses it. Presentational gap in a privacy justification rather than a false bound.
